newsitem.title: USA: UPS aims for direct electronic link with customers.
newsitem.headline: UPS aims for direct electronic link with customers.

text.p: United Parcel Services said on Wednesday that Internet technology, electronic commerce and its UPS OnLine service would remain crucial parts of its strategy of building direct connections with customers.

Based on existing infrastructure, "we're currently rolling out technology to be used directly by the customer," said Ken Lacy, who will replace Frank Erbrick as chief information officer when Erbrick retires in January 1997.
Lacy said UPS customers were getting more and more information on their packages at the point of origin, by using the company's information-based services.

The privately-held package distribution company, which budgeted $1.65 billion in 1996 for information technology, cited its recently-launched series of on-line products, including the Host Access program, which provided large customers with mainframe connections, and a trend-tracking program for smaller customers who shipped less frequently.

UPS was also planning before the end of the year to launch UPS OnLine Teleship, a program with a smart phone device that lets customers without computers tap into UPS electronic information by telephone, a UPS spokeswoman said.
As for Internet technology, UPS said it was now spending roughly $5 million to $10 million a year on Internet infrastructure, but it hoped to double or triple that figure in 1997.

"The Internet is playing a very big role in our connectivity to our customers," Erbrick said. "A great deal of money we're spending now and a lot of the resources are directed in several areas, so wherever the Internet goes, we will be there."
Putting the infrastructure in place was critical, Lacy said, and UPS had formed a team to study Internet strategy.
Electronic commerce was also imperative to the near future, the company said.

"You will not function in our business without having extensive electronic connection with customers," Erbrick said, adding that the company wanted to be the conduit for the flow of products and information.
"What we want to do is become the ubiquitous connection between you and whomever you want to talk to," he said.
UPS said it was already performing customized electronic logistics services for some of its larger customers, and it had formed a task force to study the implementation of electronic commerce.
